newsitem.title: USA: Yeltsin resurfaces in "excellent' form at G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin resurfaces in "excellent' form at G7 summit.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, who missed a late-night gala concert at the Group of Seven summit, resurfaced on Sunday looking well at a meeting with French President Jacques Chirac.
"It's good to see you in good shape. When I see you I'm always in a good mood," Chirac said at the start of the meeting. Yeltsin, he said after their talks, looked "excellent."
The 66-year-old Russian leader got out of his chair to greet Chirac without any problems and appeared fit. He spoke clearly and coherently to reporters after the meeting at his hotel.
The only sign of the ill health that kept him out of the Kremlin for the best part of eight months until February was his clear loss of weight in that time.
"Our views on international affairs are the same," Yeltsin said of the talks with Chirac. "When he speaks, it is like me speaking. When I speak, it is as if he is speaking."
Yeltsin, who has a history of mysterious disappearing acts, had at least two heart attacks last year and his absence from the concert prompted speculation about his health.

Stephanie Denning, spokeswoman for the Denver Health Medical Center, said an ambulance was sent to Yeltsin's hotel as a precaution on Saturday night after the president left a dinner with G7 leaders early.
"He was not feeling well after dinner. He went directly to his hotel. We did send an ambulance to his hotel but it was never used," she said. "He was taken care of by his personal physican."
But Russian reform chief Anatoly Chubais told NBC's Meet the Press television program that the president had simply been "a little bit tired".

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said: "It is obvious that after the hard work of the two days, plus the altitude and the heat, the president required some extra rest. In fact the other leaders could hardly fight off sleep."
Chirac made clear that he approved of Yeltsin's decision to give the concert a miss.
"You were right yesterday night," he told Yeltsin. "All the others sat down and fell asleep, especially (Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro) Hashimoto -- a very deep sleep."
Yastrzhembsky said he could confirm that Russian officials had called the hospital.

Yeltsin, who defeated a communist candidate to win a second term in office last July, spent eight months out of the Kremlin from the middle of last year after heart problems, multiple bypass surgery and then pneumonia.

He left the Saturday night dinner of G7 leaders about 20 minutes ahead of the others and skipped the gala concert. Journalists had been told that the leaders would all leave the dinner together and the concert organizers said they had expected Yeltsin to join the guests.

The Denver summit, attended by the leaders of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States, was Yeltsin's first long excursion from Russia since his recovery from heart surgery, although he has made several trips in Russia and Europe.
Denver is more than 5,000 feet (1,550 metres) high in the foothills of the Rocky Mountains and visitors are warned to acclimatize gradually because of the debilitating effects of altitude.
Yeltsin failed to show up for a meeting with Japan's foreign minister in 1992 and left Irish officials standing on the tarmac dring a stopover at Shannon airport in September 1994.
